analysis.one_liner: Cuts off all federal funding for the National Labor Relations Board.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have eliminated the agency that enforces private-sector labor law, got no cosponsors and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill says no money may be appropriated for the National Labor Relations Board, the federal agency that enforces labor law for private-sector workers. Cutting its funding would have shut down the agency's work: workers could not get elections to vote on union representation or file complaints over illegal firing during organizing drives. The bill never moved after referral to a committee and subcommittee, and Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who face NLRB complaints or who oppose union organizing at their workplaces. Without an enforcement agency, workers would have no federal forum to challenge illegal retaliation for union activity, and employers would face no practical risk of federal labor-law enforcement.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would bar any funds from being appropriated for the National Labor Relations Board, which would end the agency's operations [S3].
The stated effect is to deny any appropriations for the NLRB [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private-sector workers. The NLRB is the sole federal agency that conducts union representation elections and adjudicates claims of illegal employer conduct, so its elimination would leave workers in organizing drives or unfair-firing disputes without a federal forum, and unions would lose the enforcement backdrop for organizing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers relying on federal labor-law enforcement

drawbacks.text: A supporter of the bill would argue the NLRB's union-favorable rulings overreach, but the honest cost of this approach is that defunding eliminates all federal labor-law enforcement, not just contested rulings [S2].

Because the bill cuts off all appropriations rather than reforming any specific NLRB practice, even employers who want a functioning election process would lose it; representation elections and complaint adjudication both depend on NLRB funding [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers no replacement for the functions it eliminates. Whatever concerns motivated it could be addressed through targeted reform; a total funding cutoff would leave private-sector workers with no federal agency to run union elections or hear complaints, and would hand maximum leverage to employers who resist organizing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee and then a subcommittee with no cosponsors and no hearing, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Salmon introduced the bill on April 2, 2014 [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S5].
On June 13, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where it remained with no further action [S5].
No member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015, with the bill never having received a committee markup or floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and the NLRB. The agency kept its funding and continued enforcing labor law because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The NLRB and the workers it protects

for.name: Rep. Matt Salmon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit any appropriation of funds for the NLRB

against.name: John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or hearing on the bill, which stayed in a subcommittee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no party lineup is recorded.

industries.note: Defunding the NLRB would eliminate federal enforcement of laws against illegal firing and retaliation during organizing drives, giving such employers maximum leverage at workers' expense. The bill's gain to this interest is the public's loss.

Unions depend on NLRB-conducted representation elections and enforcement of unfair-labor-practice rules; losing the agency would make organizing far harder. Their interest here runs with workers' interests.
